translationRepairs: Coastal prefectures paid twenty thousand hu of salt a year to the Minister of Revenue in lieu of land tax.
Coastal prefectures delivered twenty thousand hu of salt a year to the Court of Imperial Granaries in lieu of land tax.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 司農 is the Minister of Agriculture / Court of the National Granaries, not the Minister of Revenue.
Coastal prefectures each year had rent remitted in exchange for twenty thousand hu of salt delivered to the Minister of Revenue.
Coastal prefectures had their annual land tax remitted in return for delivering twenty thousand hu of salt to the Court of Imperial Granaries.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 司農 is the Minister of Agriculture / Court of the National Granaries, not the Minister of Revenue.
Qing, Chu, Hai, Cang, Di, Hang, Su, and other prefectures used salt proceeds to buy light goods for delivery to the Minister of Revenue as well.
Qing, Chu, Hai, Cang, Di, Hang, Su, and other prefectures used salt proceeds to buy light goods, which they also delivered to the Court of Imperial Granaries.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 司農 is the Minister of Agriculture / Court of the National Granaries, not the Minister of Revenue.
Qing, Chu, Hai, Cang, Di, Hang, Su, and other prefectures used salt revenues to purchase light goods, which were also delivered to the Minister of Revenue.
Qing, Chu, Hai, Cang, Di, Hang, Su, and other prefectures used salt revenues to purchase light goods, which were also delivered to the Court of Imperial Granaries.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 司農 is the Minister of Agriculture / Court of the National Granaries, not the Minister of Revenue.

Yanzhou's Wuyuan had the Wu, Bai, Wa, and Xixiang ponds; Lingzhou had eight ponds including Wenquan and Huile; Huizhou had the He pond. These three prefectures all paid grain in place of salt tribute.

Yanzhou's Wuyuan had the Wu, Bai, Wa, and Xixiang ponds; Lingzhou had the Wenquan, Liangjing, Changwei, Wuquan, Hongtao, Huile, and Hongjing ponds; Huizhou had the He pond. These three prefectures all paid grain in place of salt tribute.
Chinese lists seven named Lingzhou ponds, not eight; the idiomatic paraphrase invents an eight-pond count and drops the named list. Independent source review confirms the correction.

Four production fields operated at Lianshui, Huzhou, Yuezhou, and Hangzhou, and ten supervisory posts at Jiaxing, Hailing, Yancheng, and elsewhere. Annual revenue exceeded one million strings—equivalent to taxes from more than a hundred prefectures.

Four production fields operated at Lianshui, Huzhou, Yuezhou, and Hangzhou, and ten supervisory posts at Jiaxing, Hailing, Yancheng, Xinting, Linping, Lanting, Yongjia, Dachang, Houguan, and Fudu. Annual revenue exceeded one million strings—equivalent to taxes from more than a hundred prefectures.
Chinese names all ten supervisory posts; idiomatic English replaces seven of them with 'and elsewhere'. Independent source review confirms the correction.

Li Qi lavished tribute to court his patrons and bribed senior ministers with rich gifts, hoarding salt profits privately while the treasury emptied. The monopoly system collapsed into sham valuations—of every thousand cash collected, barely one hundred thirty was real revenue.

Li Qi lavished tribute to secure favor and bribed senior ministers with rich gifts, hoarding salt profits privately while the treasury emptied. The monopoly system collapsed into sham valuations—of every thousand cash collected, barely one hundred thirty was real revenue.
'to court his patrons' is ungrammatical and misrenders 盛貢獻以固寵; the sense is lavish tribute to secure favor. Independent source review confirms the correction.
Under Zhenyuan, selling a shi of smuggled Two Ponds salt meant death; under Yuanhe the penalty was reduced to exile at Tiande and Wucheng. Huangfu Bo petitioned to restore the death penalty.
Under Zhenyuan, selling a shi of smuggled Two Ponds salt meant death; under Yuanhe the penalty was reduced to exile at the Five Forts of Tiande. Huangfu Bo petitioned to restore the death penalty.
天德五城 denotes the Five Forts of Tiande, not two places named Tiande and Wucheng. Independent source review confirms the correction.
In Zhenyuan, selling one shi of stolen Two Ponds salt was death; by Yuanhe it was reduced to exile at Tiande and Wucheng; Bo memorialized to restore death as before.
In Zhenyuan, selling one shi of stolen Two Ponds salt was death; by Yuanhe it was reduced to exile at the Five Forts of Tiande; Bo memorialized to restore death as before.
天德五城 is the Tiande Five Forts; rendering 五城 as Wucheng is incorrect. Independent source review confirms the correction.
Palace Attendant Wei Chuhou and Vice Minister Han Yu rebutted the plan point by point as unworkable, and Pingshu backed down.
Secretariat Drafter Wei Chuhou and Vice Minister Han Yu rebutted the plan point by point as unworkable, and Pingshu backed down.
中書舍人 is a Secretariat drafting attendant, not the office usually rendered Palace Attendant. Independent source review confirms the correction.
Vice Minister Lu Hongzhi, finding the Two Ponds system failing, sent patrol official Sikong Yu to draft new rules. Revenue doubled, and Lu was promoted to Salt Monopoly Commissioner.
Vice Minister Lu Hongzhi, finding the Two Ponds system failing, sent patrol official Sikong Yu to draft new rules. Revenue doubled, and Yu was promoted to Salt Monopoly Commissioner.
After 遣…司空輿更立新法，其課倍入，遷榷鹽使, the promotion most naturally refers to Sikong Yu, who established the new law. Independent source review confirms the correction.
Linghu Chu succeeded him as Salt and Tea Commissioner, restoring monopoly payments with price increases but abandoning the harshest measures.
Linghu Chu succeeded him as Salt and Iron Commissioner and also Tea Monopoly Commissioner, restoring monopoly payments with price increases only.
Idiomatic invents abandoning the harshest measures and compresses 鹽鐵使兼榷茶使; Chinese only restores monopoly dues with price increase alone. Independent source review confirms the correction.

When Xuanzong added 520,000 bolts of silk for Hexi garrisons, Pei Xiu petitioned to restore central control of mines for state revenue, adding two silver works and seventy-one iron mines while closing twenty-seven copper works and one lead mine.

When Xuanzong added 520,000 bolts of silk for Hehuang garrisons, Pei Xiu petitioned to restore central control of mines for state revenue, adding two silver works and seventy-one iron mines while closing twenty-seven copper works and one lead mine.
河湟 denotes Hehuang, not Hexi (河西); the frontier place name is mistranslated. Independent source review confirms the correction.

When Xuanzong increased Hexi garrison clothing silk by five hundred twenty thousand bolts, Transport Commissioner Pei Xiu requested return to the Salt and Iron Commissioner to supply state use; two silver smelteries and seventy-one iron mountains were added; twenty-seven copper smelteries and one lead mountain were abolished.

When Xuanzong increased Hehuang garrison clothing silk by five hundred twenty thousand bolts, Transport Commissioner Pei Xiu requested return to the Salt and Iron Commissioner to supply state use; two silver smelteries and seventy-one iron mountains were added; twenty-seven copper smelteries and one lead mountain were abolished.
河湟 should be rendered Hehuang rather than Hexi in the literal English. Independent source review confirms the correction.
In the fourth year the eastern capital sold grain, collecting one hundred debased coins per dou, which the Court Provisioner and Minister of Revenue then destroyed.
In the fourth year, the eastern capital sold grain and collected one hundred debased coins per dou; the Court of Imperial Manufactories and the Court of Imperial Granaries then destroyed them.
Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 司農 is the agricultural/treasury ministry, not the Ministry of Revenue (戶部).
In the fourth year the eastern capital was ordered to sell grain; per dou one hundred bad coins were separately collected; the Court Provisioner and Minister of Revenue destroyed them.

In the fourth year, the eastern capital was ordered to sell grain, separately collecting one hundred bad coins per dou; the Court of Imperial Manufactories and the Court of Imperial Granaries destroyed them.
Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 司農 is mistranslated as Minister of Revenue; it is not 戶部.

The debate went to the full court. Chancellor Pei Yaoji, Li Linfu, Xiao Jiong, and Cui Hao all argued that "strict suppression of bad coin, copper taxes commuted to corvée, and regulated valuations would let official mints succeed and private coin die from thin margins.

The proposal was circulated among the court officials. Chancellor Pei Yaoqing, Yellow Gate Vice Director Li Linfu, Henan Junior Prefect Xiao Jiong, and Secretariat Director Cui Mian all argued: "Strictly suppressing bad coin would make the people understand the prohibition; taxing copper and commuting labor service would enable the official mints to operate; setting valuations and labor quotas would make private coinage unprofitable and cause it to cease of itself.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 裴耀卿 is Pei Yaoqing (not Yaoji); 崔沔 is Cui Mian (not Hao); idiomatic also drops the offices given in the Chinese.

The proposal went to the hundred officials; Chancellor Pei Yaoji, Yellow Gate Vice Director Li Linfu, Henan Junior Prefect Xiao Jiong, and Secretariat Director Cui Hao all held that "if bad coins are strictly cut off people will know the ban; if copper is taxed and corvée commuted official smelting can succeed; if valuation and corvée are calculated private coin will cease of itself because profit is thin.

The proposal went to the court officials; Chancellor Pei Yaoqing, Yellow Gate Vice Director Li Linfu, Henan Junior Prefect Xiao Jiong, and Secretariat Director Cui Mian all held that "if bad coin were strictly suppressed, the people would understand the prohibition; if copper were taxed and labor service commuted, official minting could succeed; and if valuations and labor quotas were fixed, private coinage would cease of itself because the profit was slight.
Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. Same name errors: 裴耀卿→Pei Yaoqing; 崔沔→Cui Mian.
Coin debasement grows because private minting proliferates while official furnaces do not increase.
Coin had grown scarce because the population increased daily while the number of minting furnaces remained unchanged.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 錢重 means coin becomes heavy/dear, not 'debasement'; the idiomatic reverses the sense of 錢重繇人日滋於前.
Prince Li Fu of Xin'an again petitioned to allow private minting for lack of revenue; courtiers feared opposing the emperor's brother, until only Wei Boyang objected and the proposal was blocked.

Li Yi, Prince of Xin'an, again petitioned to allow private minting because state revenues were insufficient; courtiers feared opposing the emperor's brother, and only Wei Boyang objected, so the proposal was blocked.
Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 信安郡王禕 is Li Yi (禕); Fu is a mistransliteration of 禕.

Prince of Xin'an Li Fu again said state use was insufficient and requested allowing private casting; debaters all feared Fu's rank as the emperor's younger brother and dared not oppose; only Bureau of Granaries Director Wei Boyang held it impossible; Fu's proposal was also blocked.

Li Yi, Prince of Xin'an, again said that state funds were insufficient and requested permission for private minting. The officials debating the matter all feared Yi's status as the emperor's younger brother and dared not oppose him; only Bureau of Granaries Director Wei Boyang maintained that it was unworkable, and Yi's proposal was again blocked.
Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. Same 禕→Yi correction throughout the literal English.
Ninety-nine furnaces operated nationwide: thirty at Jiangzhou, ten each at Yang, Run, Xuan, E, and Yu, five each at Yi and Chen, three at Yangzhou, one at Dingzhou.
Ninety-nine furnaces operated nationwide: thirty at Jiangzhou, ten each at Yang, Run, Xuan, E, and Yu, five each at Yi and Chen, three at Yang Prefecture, and one at Dingzhou.
洋州 is Yang Prefecture (洋州), not Yangzhou (揚州); the idiomatic conflates 洋州 with 揚州. Independent source review confirms the correction.
Furnaces under Heaven numbered ninety-nine: Jiangzhou thirty; Yang, Run, Xuan, E, and Yu each ten; Yi and Chen each five; Yangzhou three; Dingzhou one.
Furnaces under Heaven numbered ninety-nine: Jiangzhou had thirty; Yang, Run, Xuan, E, and Yu each had ten; Yi and Chen each had five; Yang Prefecture had three; and Dingzhou had one.
Same 洋州≠揚州 distinction required in the literal English. Independent source review confirms the correction.
In 758, with expenses insufficient, Mint Commissioner Diwu Qi cast the Qianyuan zhongbao—one cun across, ten jin per string, valued at ten Kaiyuan coins, also called the "ten-for" coin.

In Suzong's first year of Qianyuan (758), with expenses insufficient, Mint Commissioner Diwu Qi cast the Qianyuan zhongbao—one cun across, ten jin per string, valued at ten Kaiyuan coins, also called the "ten-for" coin.
Idiomatic omits 肅宗 present in the Chinese and reduces the reign date to a bare Western year. Independent source review confirms the correction.

With young and old evenly distributed and two sheng of rice per person daily, annual consumption reached 45.36 million hu; clothing doubled that, ritual expenses doubled again, and three years' reserves for disaster required 1.36 billion hu—at which rice and coin would balance in value.

With young and old evenly distributed and two sheng of rice per person daily, daily consumption was 1.26 million hu and annual consumption 453.6 million hu; clothing doubled that, ritual expenses doubled again, and three years' reserves for disaster required 1.3608 billion hu—at which rice and coin would balance in value.
Chinese 歲費四萬五千三百六十萬斛 is 453.6 million hu, not 45.36 million; the idiomatic figure drops a factor of ten and omits the stated daily total. Independent source review confirms the correction.

Young and strong evenly distributed, each person ate two sheng of rice daily—one million two hundred sixty thousand hu per day, forty-five million three hundred sixty thousand hu yearly; clothing doubled this, auspicious and inauspicious rites doubled again; leaving three years' storage against flood, drought, and disaster required one billion three hundred sixty million eight hundred thousand hu of rice; with noble and base, plenty and want balanced, then rice's value and coin would be equal.

Young and strong evenly distributed, each person ate two sheng of rice daily—one million two hundred sixty thousand hu per day, four hundred fifty-three million six hundred thousand hu yearly; clothing doubled this, auspicious and inauspicious rites doubled again; leaving three years' storage against flood, drought, and disaster required one billion three hundred sixty million eight hundred thousand hu of rice; with noble and base, plenty and want balanced, then rice's value and coin would be equal.
四萬五千三百六十萬斛 means 453,600,000 hu; the literal yearly figure understates by a factor of ten. Independent source review confirms the correction.

In the twelfth year the metropolitan government received five hundred thousand strings to buy silk; hoarders with over five thousand strings faced death; princes' illicit purchases were confiscated with one-fifth to informers.

In the twelfth year, the metropolitan government received five hundred thousand strings to buy cloth and silk. Wealthy households holding more than five thousand strings faced death; princes and dukes were heavily demoted and their property confiscated, with one-fifth awarded to informers.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 王公重貶，沒入於官 means princes and dukes were heavily demoted and property confiscated; the idiomatic 'princes' illicit purchases were confiscated' misreads 重貶 as illicit purchasing.
In 829 an edict required Buddha images of lead, tin, earth, or wood, with gold and silver ornament only; copper was limited to mirrors, chimes, nails, rings, and buttons—counterfeiters faced death.

In 829 an edict required Buddha images of lead, tin, earth, or wood; ornamental bands might use gold, silver, brass, black oil, and blue iron; copper was limited to mirrors, chimes, nails, rings, and buttons—illicit casters faced death.
Idiomatic omits 鍮石、烏油、藍鐵 among allowed ornament materials and flattens them to gold and silver only. Independent source review confirms the correction.

When Wuzong suppressed Buddhism, mint official Li Yuyan petitioned to confiscate copper statues, bells, chimes, censers, and clappers for the patrol office, greatly increasing copper supplies in the prefectures.

When Wuzong suppressed Buddhism, Yongping mint official Li Yuyan requested that copper statues, bells, chimes, censers, and clappers be confiscated for the patrol offices, greatly increasing the prefectures' copper supplies.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. Idiomatic English omits 永平 from 永平監官; the literal correctly keeps Yongping as the mint designation.
Huainan governor Li Shen proposed minting coin named by prefecture—capital coin for the capital, one cun like Kaiyuan tongbao, with old coin banned in trade.
Huainan military governor Li Shen proposed minting coin named by prefecture—capital coin for the capital, one cun like Kaiyuan tongbao, with old coin banned in trade.
節度使 is a military governor; idiomatic “governor” understates the office that the literal renders as military governor. Independent source review confirms the correction.
